title: WCAG: Web Accessibility Guidelines Explained
description: WCAG explained for business owners: what levels A, AA and AAA mean, what changed in WCAG 2.2, a worked checkout example, and the mistakes we see most.
name: WCAG
lead: WCAG is the international standard for making websites usable by people with disabilities, including people who use screen readers, keyboards instead of a mouse, magnification or captions. It is published by the W3C and is the yardstick most accessibility rules point to.

facts.label: Published by
facts.value: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Web Accessibility Initiative

facts.label: Backward compatibility
facts.value: Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0

facts.label: New in WCAG 2.2
facts.value: 9 new success criteria, including Target Size (Minimum) at 24 by 24 CSS pixels; 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete

body: WCAG is a list of testable success criteria grouped under four principles: content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. Each criterion has a level. Level A covers the basics without which some people cannot use a page at all. Level AA adds a further set and is the level most often set as a target. Level AAA is the strictest and is rarely required for a whole site.

The current version is WCAG 2.2, published in October 2023. It added 9 criteria, several aimed at people with motor and cognitive disabilities, and retired the old Parsing criterion. Because the versions are backward compatible, meeting 2.2 also means meeting 2.1 and 2.0.

A Victoria gift shop tests its checkout with a keyboard only. The cart button can't be reached with the Tab key, the focus outline has been removed in the theme's styles, and the error message for a wrong postal code is shown only in red text. Each of those fails a WCAG criterion.

The fixes are small: make the cart a real button, restore a visible focus style, and write the error in words next to the field. On phones, the shop also enlarges the tiny quantity buttons so they meet the new minimum target size of 24 by 24 CSS pixels in WCAG 2.2.

sections.h2: Where it matters for a Canadian small business
body: Accessibility rules in parts of Canada point to WCAG, and the version, the level and who must comply differ by jurisdiction. Check the rules for your province and sector rather than assuming; our accessibility law guides cite the official sources.
Aside from the law, an accessible checkout and booking form simply lose fewer customers, including older visitors and anyone on a small screen.
Most failures we find on small business sites come from the theme or from images, not from complex code.
list: Images with no text alternative, or alt text that just repeats the file name.
Light grey text on white that fails contrast.
Forms whose fields have no visible labels, only placeholder text.
Buttons and menus that only work with a mouse.
Relying on an overlay widget instead of fixing the underlying pages.

checklist: Use your site with only the keyboard: Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space.
Check that every form field has a visible label and clear error text.
Review alt text on your home page and top product or service pages.
Test text contrast with a free checker on your main colour combinations.

faqs.q: Which WCAG level should my site meet?
faqs.a: Level AA is the usual target. Check the specific rule that applies to you, since some name a particular version.

faqs.q: Is WCAG 2.2 harder to meet than 2.1?
faqs.a: It adds 9 criteria, so there is more to check, but most are practical things like target size, visible focus and not forcing people to re-enter information.
